newsitem.title: UK: SPORTS TO CASH IN ON GROWTH IN TELEVISION CHANNELS.
newsitem.headline: SPORTS TO CASH IN ON GROWTH IN TELEVISION CHANNELS.

text.p: Rapid growth in the number of television channels in Europe will ensure rich pickings for the sports world in coming years, but some risk missing out on the cash bonanza, delegates told a conference on Wednesday.
Television executives said the extra channel capacity created by digital television would put an even greater premium on the rights to top quality sports events.
"Sports events will be even more sought after than in the past," Dieter Hahn, managing director of Germany's DSF sports channel told the "Sports and Television" conference.
"In an environment of hundreds of channels, sports events will provide one of the few programming elements by which broadcasters can easily distinguish themselves," he added.

The value of sports rights has increased repeatedly over the past decade as satellite companies muscle into an area which was once largely the preserve of public service broadcasters such as the BBC, Germany's ZDF and ARD and Italy's RAI.
This trend is set to continue with the advent of digital technology, multiplying the number of channels and making pay-per-view events a viable option.

France and Italy have already introduced pay-per-view soccer while Britain's BSkyB screened the Mike Tyson-Evander Holyfield heavyweight title fight on that basis last weekend in its second such experiment .
But sports were warned that they would end up poor relations if they failed to tailor their product to television audiences.
"I am certain that many sports will fail to deliver and to innovate to television's needs," said Bill Sinrich, senior vice-president of Trans World International (TWI).
"Revenue will be concentrated in the hands of a select number of sports," Sinrich added.
TWI is the television production arm of American Mark McCormack's IMG sports marketing agency.
Sinrich said he was not advocating controversial rule changes such as the introduction of "time-outs" to allow more advertising during soccer matches.

But he said sports must be prepared to alter their schedules to allow matches to be screened live so the largest audience can be reached, as has happened with league soccer in countries such as England, Italy and Germany.

Sinrich said that British athletics had been badly damaged by its failure to ensure the presence of top stars during televised meetings. This had led broadcasters increasingly to turn their backs on the sport.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which groups public service broadcasters across the continent, renewed the call for action to stop the migration of top events to pay channels.
"I believe sport has a cultural place in society and must be protected," said Richard Bunn, head of sport at the EBU.
The European Parliament on Tuesday agreed to press for rules to ensure that terrestrial television viewers retain access to major events even if they are snapped up by pay-TV operators.
